articles.title: Expert Witness Barred from Practice During Letby Trial Not Disclosed to Jury
articles.summary: A senior paediatric endocrinologist whose testimony helped convict Lucy Letby was barred from treating patients during the trial, a fact jurors were never told, according to The Guardian.
articles.content:
Prof Peter Hindmarsh, a consultant paediatric endocrinologist and professor at University College London, played a central role in the Crown's case against neonatal nurse Lucy Letby. His specialist knowledge of hormones, including insulin, was used to argue that Letby had poisoned infants by injecting insulin into intravenous fluid bags. The prosecution presented his testimony as decisive, and the lead Crown barrister, Nick Johnson KC, introduced him to the jury as “the pre-eminent expert”.

During the same period, Hindmarsh was subject to a series of professional concerns raised by his employer, University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust (UCLH), and the General Medical Council (GMC). In March 2023, UCLH formally barred him from treating patients, citing an unacceptable level of risk to children and young people. The decision followed internal reports that his advice on insulin and diabetes management for child patients was deemed unsafe. A medical director at UCLH, Dr Tim Hodgson, wrote to the GMC that “On the grounds of safety UCLH are not presently in a position to allow Professor [Hindmarsh] to practice clinically even under supervision”.

The GMC had already opened an investigation into Hindmarsh’s fitness to practise after earlier concerns were raised by Great Ormond Street Hospital and UCLH in late 2022. While the regulator sought to suspend his registration, an independent medical tribunal in April 2023 declined to impose a suspension. Instead, the tribunal ordered that Hindmarsh be directly supervised when treating patients, a measure that became moot once UCLH excluded him from clinical duties altogether.

The exclusion occurred after Hindmarsh gave his final day of evidence at the Letby trial on 24 February 2023. The jury, however, was never informed that his employing hospital had concluded his professional judgment posed a safety risk, nor that a tribunal had ruled on his supervision requirements. The Crown Prosecution Service disclosed to Letby’s defence that Hindmarsh was under a GMC investigation, but did not reveal the subsequent barring or the tribunal’s decision. Legal experts note that failure to disclose such information could breach the criminal procedure rules that require expert witnesses to inform the instructing party of any disciplinary proceedings or factors that might undermine credibility.

If Letby’s defence had been aware of the hospital’s concerns, they might have challenged Hindmarsh’s credibility and sought to have his evidence excluded or the jury instructed accordingly. The lack of disclosure has been highlighted as a potential ground for referral to the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC), the body that investigates possible miscarriages of justice.

Letby was convicted of murdering seven infants and attempting to murder seven others at the Countess of Chester Hospital, receiving fifteen whole‑life orders. She has consistently maintained her innocence, and her legal team, led by Mark McDonald, has applied to the CCRC to have the case reconsidered. Since the convictions, a number of leading medical experts, both in the UK and internationally, have contested the prosecution’s scientific basis, arguing that the evidence of insulin poisoning was flawed.

One such expert, Dr Shoo Lee, a Canadian neonatologist, convened a panel that concluded the infants died from natural causes and suboptimal care, finding no evidence of deliberate insulin administration. Additional experts supporting the CCRC application have criticised Hindmarsh’s calculations and diagnoses, stating that his hypothesis of insulin being infused via fluid bags was not supported by the medical record. They also point to the fallibility of immunoassay blood tests, which the prosecution presented as definitive proof of insulin poisoning, noting that such tests can give falsely high insulin results.

Background: In criminal trials, expert witnesses provide specialised opinions that can influence juries on complex scientific or medical matters. Under the criminal procedure rules, experts must disclose any ongoing investigations, disciplinary actions, or other issues that could affect their impartiality or the weight of their testimony. Failure to do so may lead to challenges on the admissibility of their evidence and can form the basis for appeals or reviews.

Background: Insulin is a hormone that regulates blood glucose levels. In children, inappropriate insulin administration can cause hypoglycaemia, a dangerous drop in blood sugar, while insufficient insulin leads to hyperglycaemia and can trigger diabetic ketoacidosis, a life‑threatening condition. Determining whether insulin was deliberately introduced into a patient’s fluid bag requires careful analysis of clinical signs, laboratory tests, and the context of treatment.

The tribunal that reviewed Hindmarsh’s case acknowledged that the three incidents identified by UCLH raised patient‑safety concerns, yet concluded that suspending his registration would be disproportionate. The panel allowed him to continue non‑clinical work, including acting as an expert witness, while tightening supervision requirements for any clinical activity. In practice, however, Hindmarsh was already prevented from seeing patients, rendering the supervisory order largely theoretical.

Hindmarsh’s own statements at the trial asserted that blood tests and medical records of two infants indicated insulin poisoning, most likely through intravenous fluid bags. The prosecution framed this as incontrovertible evidence, and the jury returned guilty verdicts on the attempted‑murder charges for those two cases, marking the first unanimous guilty findings in the trial.

The judge, James Goss, summed up by telling jurors that if they were convinced the babies had been deliberately harmed, they could infer that other infants were also victims, even without certainty about the precise mechanism. This instruction underscored the weight given to Hindmarsh’s testimony.

Documents obtained by The Guardian reveal that UCLH’s concerns were communicated to the GMC on 15 March 2023, shortly after Hindmarsh completed his courtroom testimony. The hospital’s medical director noted that Hindmarsh had breached a supervision order by offering independent medical advice to families of three child patients, two of which involved insulin and diabetes management. In one instance, he advised families to stop insulin at home, a recommendation that coincided with an episode of diabetic ketoacidosis, a severe complication caused by a lack of insulin.

The director also highlighted that Hindmarsh appeared to focus on rare causes of hypoglycaemia and diabetes, potentially overlooking more common explanations. Colleagues expressed concern that he was not addressing typical causes of high glucose levels appropriately. These clinical judgments formed part of the rationale for the hospital’s decision to bar him from practice.

Hindmarsh’s barrister argued that, because he was no longer treating patients, his ability to serve as an expert witness should not be impeded by a suspension. The tribunal ultimately agreed, allowing him to continue in that capacity while maintaining the supervisory requirement for any clinical work.

The case raises broader questions about the transparency of expert witness disclosures in high‑profile criminal trials. Legal commentators note that undisclosed disciplinary actions can affect the fairness of a trial, especially when the expert’s testimony is pivotal to the prosecution’s narrative. The potential for a CCRC referral underscores the seriousness with which the justice system treats such procedural lapses.

As the CCRC reviews Letby’s application, the undisclosed restriction on Hindmarsh’s clinical practice remains a focal point. Should the commission find that the non‑disclosure compromised the trial’s integrity, it could recommend a referral to the Court of Appeal, potentially altering the outcome of a case that has already resulted in multiple whole‑life sentences.

articles.title: US Navy Official Claims $64 Million Insurance for Hormuz Transit Amid Conflict
articles.summary: A senior US Navy official said insurance for a single commercial crossing of the Strait of Hormuz has risen to $64 million, a figure unverified and far above earlier estimates, as the waterway remains partially closed by the Iran‑US conflict.
articles.content:
Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao told a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing that the cost of insuring a commercial vessel for one passage through the Strait of Hormuz now stands at $64 million. He contrasted this with a pre‑war figure of $54,000, indicating a dramatic increase since the United States and Israel began strikes on Iran on 28 February. Cao’s statement was made while lawmakers questioned the broader financial impact of the conflict on freedom of navigation.

The claim has not been independently corroborated. Analysts note that the $64 million number appears unusually high even by wartime standards. Michelle Bockmann of maritime‑intelligence firm Windward asked whether the figure reflects war‑risk premiums calculated as a percentage of a ship’s hull value, a method that can produce widely varying totals depending on vessel type and cargo. A July report from S&P Global indicated that war‑risk premiums had risen to between 7.5 and 10 percent of hull value, up from 1 to 3 percent before the conflict. Applying those rates to a large crude tanker could generate a premium of roughly $21 million, according to that analysis. Reuters later reported that the overall cost of moving oil through Hormuz had climbed to about $10 million‑$20 million per cargo.

Regardless of the exact figure, the surge in insurance costs reflects the heightened danger that ships face in the narrow waterway. War‑risk insurance protects vessels against loss from missiles, drones, naval mines or other military actions, and its price is tied to the vessel’s value, the cargo it carries, and the perceived likelihood of attack. Higher premiums can ripple through freight rates, fuel prices and the price of goods worldwide.

The strait, the only sea route linking the Persian Gulf with the Arabian Sea and the open ocean, historically handled about one‑fifth of global oil supplies. Since the February strikes, Iran has effectively limited passage, allowing only selected ships and targeting those it deems unauthorized. The resulting restrictions have contributed to shortages of oil, gas, fertiliser and other essential products that normally flow through the corridor.

Shipping activity remains far below pre‑war levels. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) recorded 308 vessel crossings in the week ending 11 November, a drop of roughly 65 percent from the volume seen before the conflict. Of those, 139 were outbound and 169 inbound. Recent incidents underscore the ongoing hazards: UKMTO reported two tanker attacks, including one near Oman that left a vessel disabled and its engine room ablaze, and Iranian forces later claimed three additional tankers had struck naval mines.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly asserted that the United States has secured the strait, citing naval escorts and a blockade of Iranian ports. Iran, however, maintains that it controls passage and requires vessels to follow approved routes coordinated with its forces. It has granted exemptions for ships from India, China, Iraq and Qatar, but the approved lanes bring vessels much closer to the Iranian coastline than before.

During the hearing, Cao also described the strain the war has placed on the US Navy, noting prolonged deployments and deteriorating conditions for service members. He said, "This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy," highlighting concerns about crew welfare. Democrats on the panel challenged his remarks, accusing him of downplaying mental‑health issues after a series of suicide attempts on an aircraft carrier.

Background: War‑risk insurance is a specialized policy that covers losses arising from armed conflict, including damage from weapons, sabotage or capture. Insurers assess the risk based on factors such as the vessel’s size, the value of its cargo, the geopolitical environment and the likelihood of hostile action in the area of operation. Premiums can fluctuate rapidly as the security situation evolves, and they are typically added to the baseline hull and protection‑and‑indemnity coverage that ships carry for routine commercial risks.

Background: The Strait of Hormuz is a strategic chokepoint that connects the oil‑rich Persian Gulf with the wider world. Because a large share of the world’s petroleum passes through this narrow passage, any disruption can have outsized effects on global energy markets. Nations with maritime interests monitor traffic through the strait closely, and naval forces from multiple countries have historically operated there to ensure safe passage for commercial shipping.

Analysts caution that even if insurance premiums reach $20 million or more, the fundamental issue is the risk of vessels being struck by missiles, drones or mines. Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at IG, told Al Jazeera that the waterway "is only open for business if mariners are prepared to take these risks, and it certainly isn’t open by any pre‑war definition of the word." He added that the situation remains a "miracle" that a full energy crisis has been avoided so far, but warned that prolonged instability would push the development of alternative routes and supply chains.

The divergent narratives from Washington and Tehran illustrate the contested nature of the strait’s status. While US officials emphasize naval escorts and a continued flow of commerce, Iranian statements stress control over the passage and the necessity for ships to adhere to its routing demands. The combination of elevated insurance costs, reduced traffic volumes and recent attacks suggests that the strait is far from the freely navigable corridor it once was, and that the economic ramifications of the conflict continue to reverberate across global trade networks.

articles.title: Bucs face Lions as Mayfield’s status uncertain and Hutchinson out
articles.summary: Detroit’s defense is missing key players, including Aidan Hutchinson, while Tampa Bay’s offense may be without starter Baker Mayfield, setting up a clash of a strong defense versus a struggling offense, according to CBS Sports.
articles.content:
The upcoming game at Ford Field pits a Detroit team that boasts the offensive talent to contend for a championship against a Tampa Bay squad whose recent defensive play has been among the league’s best. The contest is scheduled for a 1 p.m. ET kickoff on Fox, and the indoor venue eliminates any weather factor.

Detroit’s attack has been praised as capable of winning a Super Bowl, yet the Lions have struggled to keep their defensive unit on the field. Over the past three seasons the defense has missed a total of 429 games, the highest total in the NFL. The core group that includes Aidan Hutchinson, linebacker Jack Campbell, and secondary players Brian Branch, Kerby Joseph and Alim McNeill has been plagued by injuries, and all are under 27 years old.

Hutchinson, who leads the league in pressures with 351 since 2022 and recorded 50 this season, was a third‑favorite for Defensive Player of the Year at +1100 odds before his season‑ending broken tibia and fibula. The 2024 season saw him appear in only five games before that injury, and this marks the second season‑ending injury for him in three years. The loss of his pass‑rush ability has been a major blow to Detroit’s defensive identity.

Campbell’s future is also in doubt after a neck injury suffered on Nov. 1 against Minnesota, and Joseph is slated to make his first appearance of the season after spending time on the PUP list because of a chronic knee problem that kept him out for the final 11 games of the previous year. The other two secondary members have returned, but the five‑player core has combined for 62 missed games since 2024 and has shared the field for just four of the Lions’ 43 games, representing roughly 3 % of the team’s defensive snaps.

Statistically, the Lions’ defense has been ineffective when not applying pressure. Since Week 5, the unit ranks 27th in defensive success rate, allowing a completion percentage that exceeds expectation by 3.1 percentage points, well above the league average. In contrast, when the defense does generate pressure, opponents struggle to complete passes.

Despite the defensive setbacks, Detroit has performed well enough to stay competitive. The Lions recently defeated a strong Patriots team and improved to a 7‑2 record. Their odds to win the NFC North sit at +220, while the chance to capture the conference title is listed at +870. The franchise’s odds to win the Super Bowl have slipped from +1800 to +2200, and the betting line to make the playoffs moved from -330 to -600 after the New England game.

The Buccaneers, currently 3‑6 after a bye week, need a win to keep any postseason hopes alive. They sit a single game behind first‑place Carolina in the NFC South, hold the tiebreaker, and host the Panthers in Week 12. Tampa Bay’s defense leads the league in takeaways (21), rushing yards allowed (79.1 YPG), and defensive EPA per game (10.7). It is the only team in NFL history to allow fewer than 80 rushing yards per game, record 15 or more interceptions, and remain below .500 through Week 10.

Baker Mayfield’s performance has been a focal point for the Buccaneers. In his first six starts, he has accumulated seven turnovers and posted only 925 passing yards with three passing touchdowns, a rarity in the past decade. His expected points added per dropback stands at -0.28, the fourth‑worst among qualified quarterbacks this season, trailing only a few historically poor outings. Mayfield has also been sacked on 37.5 % of dropbacks when pressured, the second‑highest rate for a qualified quarterback over the past ten seasons.

Mayfield’s availability for Sunday remains uncertain after a foot injury in Week 9. Reports indicate he "seems to be trending" toward sitting out, and the Buccaneers have added Cooper Rush to the practice squad and signed Easton Stick to the active roster. If Mayfield is unable to play, undrafted rookie Jalen Daniels, who is 1‑2 as a starter, could receive the start.

In the NFL, a defensive success rate measures how often a defense prevents an offense from achieving a positive gain on a play, while the PUP (physically unable to perform) list allows teams to retain players who are recovering from injuries without counting against the active roster limit. These mechanisms help clubs manage roster health over a long season.

The matchup offers a clear contrast: Detroit’s high‑powered offense faces a Buccaneers defense that excels at creating turnovers and limiting the run, while Tampa Bay’s offense, potentially without its starting quarterback, must rely on limited production against a Lions defense that struggles without its pass rush. CBS Sports provided the underlying data and analysis that shape this preview.

articles.title: Anthropic founders poised to become multi‑billionaires after US IPO
articles.summary: Seven former OpenAI staff who launched Anthropic will see their stakes valued at billions of dollars as the AI firm lists on a US exchange, with shares priced between $70 and $78.
articles.content:
Anthropic, the artificial‑intelligence company behind the Claude platform, is preparing to float on a US stock exchange after a rapid rise from a little‑known start‑up to a firm valued at more than a trillion dollars. The offering will price shares between $70 and $78, and at the top of that range each of the seven founders could see a paper wealth of at least $18.5 billion. The founders, all in their thirties or forties, left OpenAI in 2021 to build the new venture and now stand to become some of the wealthiest tech entrepreneurs in the world.

The company’s chief executive is Dario Amodei, 43, who previously worked at OpenAI, Baidu and Google. He departed OpenAI after growing concerns that profit motives were outweighing safety considerations. His sister, Daniela Amodei, 39, joined him in the move and now serves as Anthropic’s president, overseeing the executive team and the firm’s research, engineering, product, governance and commercial activities. In her view, her brother makes the company "ambitious". Daniela’s background includes a degree in English literature, a stint in a congressional office, and a senior role in risk operations at Stripe.

Tom Brown, also 39, followed the Amodei siblings to Anthropic after leading GPT‑3 engineering at OpenAI and working on DeepMind at Google. He now holds the title of chief compute officer, responsible for securing and deploying the computing power that underpins the firm’s models. Brown has publicly supported the view that data‑centre development can be "an enormous source of prosperity".

Jack Clark, 37, is the only non‑North‑American among the founders. Hailing from Brighton in the United Kingdom, he studied English literature and creative writing before becoming a technology journalist for outlets such as ZDNet UK, The Register and Bloomberg. At OpenAI he moved from communications to policy, and at Anthropic he leads the public‑benefit arm and heads the Anthropic Institute, an internal think‑tank focused on the societal impact of AI.

Jared Kaplan, 42, serves as chief science officer and directs Anthropic’s technical research. He holds a PhD in physics from Harvard and is an associate professor at Johns Hopkins University. Kaplan’s research on scaling laws—mathematical relationships that predict how larger AI models behave when trained on more data—has provided a framework that many AI firms use to anticipate model performance.

Chris Olah, 34, is described as the interpretability research lead, concentrating on how AI models interact and on the moral dimensions of artificial intelligence. Prior to Anthropic he led interoperability research at OpenAI and worked as a research scientist at Google Brain. Over the past year he has organized meetings with faith leaders from diverse religious traditions, exploring how moral concepts intersect with AI development.

Sam McCandlish, 36, occupies the role of chief architect, shaping Anthropic’s policies aimed at mitigating AI risks. He previously worked on safety at OpenAI and holds a physics PhD from Stanford as well as a mathematics and physics degree from Brandeis University. McCandlish will own roughly 1.6 percent of Anthropic after the share sale, positioning his stake to become a highly valuable asset.

The upcoming public offering marks a significant milestone for Anthropic, which was founded by the seven individuals after they collectively left OpenAI in 2021. Their combined expertise spans physics, computer science, policy, journalism and risk management, reflecting a multidisciplinary approach to building AI systems that prioritize safety and societal benefit.

Background: An initial public offering (IPO) allows a private company to sell shares to public investors for the first time, providing liquidity to early stakeholders and raising capital for further growth. The price range set for the shares determines the market valuation of the company and directly influences the net worth of shareholders based on the number of shares they hold.

Background: In the field of artificial intelligence, safety research focuses on ensuring that advanced models behave as intended and do not produce harmful outcomes. Techniques such as interpretability, which seeks to make model decisions understandable, and scaling law analysis, which predicts model performance as size increases, are central to this effort.

According to BBC News, the founders’ holdings will translate into multi‑billion‑dollar fortunes once the shares begin trading, assuming the highest price point is achieved. The valuation underscores the rapid financial ascent of AI firms that combine cutting‑edge technology with a pronounced emphasis on safety and public benefit.

articles.title: Portugal clinches win as Forbs scores in No 7 shirt, Wales fall short
articles.summary: Portugal secured a win over Wales after Carlos Forbs scored in the updated No 7 jersey, while Wales face a Nations League relegation playoff.
articles.content:
Portugal broke the dead‑lock in a tightly contested friendly after substitute Carlos Forbs, wearing the newly altered No 7 shirt, finished from close range in the second half. The match, played in Braga, saw the Portuguese side endure the dismissal of Pedro Neto, who received two yellow cards within minutes of each other. Despite the numerical disadvantage, Portugal held on and claimed victory, marking the first win in the post‑Ronaldo era for the iconic number.

Wales entered the game with Craig Bellamy at the helm, aware that a loss would push the nation toward a Nations League relegation playoff in March. The draw for that playoff, to be held in Switzerland, could pit Wales against Slovenia, Hungary, the Republic of Ireland or Bosnia and Herzegovina – the latter having eliminated them from World Cup qualifying earlier in the year. Bellamy stressed the need for Wales to test themselves against stronger opposition to foster development.

"If we want to develop as a football nation and continue to move forward, we have to be playing against the best teams," Bellamy said, highlighting his belief that regular competition with top sides is essential for progress. He also confirmed that his contract ends after Euro 2028, meaning he will not be in charge for the upcoming Nations League campaign.

The opening stages were lively. Bruno Fernandes put Portugal ahead after eleven minutes with a precise strike into the top corner. Wales responded swiftly; David Brooks, who had previously impressed in Norway, equalised two minutes later with a deft left‑foot finish after a quick exchange with Rubin Colwill, who later squared the ball back to Brooks for the goal. The home side reclaimed the lead shortly before the break when Sorba Thomas finished a well‑worked move, only for Pedro Neto to level the score by converting a cross from Francisco Trincão after a brief duel with Jay Dasilva.

The second half remained open. Harry Wilson, operating from midfield, produced a speculative long‑range effort that skimmed the underside of Diogo Costa’s crossbar, underscoring Portugal’s defensive vulnerabilities after a heavy defeat to Denmark the previous weekend. Wilson also had a chance that was saved by Costa before Rubin Colwill’s quick reaction led to Brooks’ second goal, this time into the far corner.

Portugal introduced João Félix and the Club Brugge winger Forbs as the match progressed. Forbs, wearing the No 7 shirt that now bears a cross through the number to honour Cristiano Ronaldo’s legacy, made an immediate impact. After a loose header from Ben Cabango fell to his feet, he advanced past a defender and placed a low finish past the goalkeeper, sealing the win for Portugal.

Wales displayed moments of promise, with Ben Cabango’s header prompting a desperate block from Costa and a header from Cabango that forced a corner. Midfielder Josh Sheehan, playing a deeper role, partnered with Colwill, while Aaron Collins made his debut after coming on from the bench. Despite the spirited performance, Wales could not find a third equaliser.

"Look, it’s a £1.2bn squad against a £170m squad," Bellamy remarked after the final whistle, acknowledging the disparity in resources and expressing satisfaction with his team’s effort despite the loss.

Background: The UEFA Nations League is a competition designed to replace many international friendlies with more competitive matches, offering promotion and relegation between leagues based on performance. Teams that finish at the bottom of their groups may face a playoff to avoid dropping to a lower tier, which can affect future fixtures and development pathways.

Background: The No 7 shirt has long been associated with Portugal’s most celebrated forward, Cristiano Ronaldo. Following his retirement from international duty, the Portuguese Football Federation introduced a version of the jersey with a diagonal line through the number, symbolising the continuation of his legacy while allowing a new player to inherit the iconic number.

Portugal’s win moves them forward as group winners, while Wales must regroup ahead of the upcoming relegation playoff, hoping to secure a place in the higher tier of the Nations League for the next cycle.

articles.title: UK Ministers Extend Palantir NHS Contract Until 2029 Before Switching to British Suppliers
articles.summary: The Department of Health and Social Care will keep Palantir's data platform contract for two more years, aiming to replace it with UK firms by 2029 amid political and ethical criticism.
articles.content:
The Department of Health and Social Care (DHSC) has announced that the NHS in England will continue using Palantir Technologies' federated data platform (FDP) for another two years, postponing the termination of the agreement until 2029. The decision follows pressure from opposition parties, campaign groups and health officials to end the partnership with the US‑based firm earlier.

Palantir, founded by Peter Thiel, a known supporter of former US President Donald Trump, provides the software that links disparate health‑care providers, allowing data to flow across hospitals, clinics and other NHS entities. The FDP is intended to create a single, searchable view of patient information, but many trusts have been reluctant to adopt it. NHS England recently removed a claim that 137 trusts were benefiting from the platform after reporting showed that only 29 trusts were using it regularly.

James Frith, a health minister, explained that the extension is meant to give the government time to identify and procure British technology firms that can take over the role. He told MPs, "The current contract will remain for two years, before coming to an end," signalling a phased approach that aims to preserve service continuity while seeking alternatives.

Opposition voices have condemned the delay. Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology select committee, said, "My committee has repeatedly called on the government to exercise the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s federated data platform contract with the NHS," reflecting frustration that the break clause will not be triggered as originally scheduled.

Liberal Democrat MP Martin Wrigley echoed the sentiment, noting that the extension keeps a company linked to a Trump ally and criticised by human‑rights organisations in control of health data for several more years. He highlighted concerns about Palantir's work with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and its alleged support for military operations.

Campaign groups such as Amnesty International and Just Treatment have long urged the government to activate the break clause. Amnesty described the eventual decision to end the contract as “a victory for healthcare workers, patients and campaigners who refused to give up,” while its crisis campaigner Tom Guha warned that the NHS should not partner with a firm involved in activities he described as supporting genocide.

Within Parliament, Labour member Ben Coleman of the health select committee welcomed the move away from a single supplier, calling Palantir an “albatross” that must be replaced without disrupting patient care or creating a new monopoly.

The DHSC has indicated that it will soon invite UK technology companies to bid for the future contract. Officials stressed that the process must earn both public trust and clinical confidence, acknowledging the scepticism among hospital leaders and clinicians regarding Palantir's promised benefits.

Background: A federated data platform aggregates information from multiple, often independent, databases into a unified system without requiring each source to store all data centrally. This approach can improve data accessibility for clinicians while preserving local control over records.

Background: A break clause in a contract allows one party to terminate the agreement before its scheduled end date, usually under specified conditions. Exercising such a clause can provide flexibility but may also entail penalties or transition challenges.

The Guardian reported on the DHSC's decision, noting that the extension was chosen over an immediate termination that could have occurred in the spring. The move is framed as a pragmatic step to avoid service disruption while the government prepares a domestically sourced replacement for the FDP.

Critics argue that the two‑year extension still leaves the NHS dependent on a foreign supplier whose ethical record has been questioned. They point to the limited uptake of the platform across trusts as evidence that the system has not delivered the expected improvements.

Supporters of the extension argue that a rushed termination could jeopardise data integration projects that are already underway, potentially affecting patient care continuity. They contend that a measured transition period allows for thorough testing of new solutions and smoother migration of sensitive health data.

The upcoming procurement process will be closely watched by both industry observers and civil‑society groups, as it will determine whether the NHS can shift to a home‑grown digital infrastructure that meets security, ethical and performance standards.

articles.title: Ministers Lack Cost Estimate for Repairing Failing NHS Maternity Units
articles.summary: NHS officials say nearly half of England’s maternity and neonatal units fail safety standards, while ministers admit they cannot quantify the expense of needed repairs.
articles.content:
NHS leaders have warned that 43% of maternity and neonatal units across England fall short of basic safety standards, a shortfall that they say hampers the delivery of clinical care thousands of times each year. The shortfall is linked to ageing buildings, leaking roofs, inadequate temperature control and cramped spaces that impede modern medical practice.

The Care Quality Commission has highlighted that insufficient space, outdated facilities and a shortage of operating theatres create serious safety risks for mothers and babies. Its assessments point to a pattern of structural deficiencies that threaten the safe provision of maternity services.

Liberal Democrat health spokesperson Helen Morgan criticised the government for not knowing the financial scale of the problem. She said, "It is appalling that, despite those warnings, the government still has no idea how much it would cost to make every maternity unit fit for purpose." Health minister Karin Smyth confirmed that the Department of Health and Social Care cannot provide a cost figure for the repairs or replacements required for units deemed at risk of imminent breakdown.

A review of Musgrove Park Hospital’s maternity department in Taunton described the building as old and unsuited to 21st‑century care, noting leaking roofs and temperature extremes that left rooms too hot or too cold. The antenatal ward required metal poles for support, and CQC inspections later identified water ingress and mould on the post‑natal ward walls and ceilings, although staff care was rated as good.

At Stepping Hill Hospital in Stockport, a birth was witnessed by a father who had to hold a loose ceiling light for an hour while his wife delivered. The light fell close to a midwife, underscoring the precarious state of the 121‑year‑old facility, which the chief executive says needs £400 million to bring it up to safe standards.

NHS England’s review of maternity and neonatal infrastructure, published in September 2025, found a clear link between the condition of physical assets and the safety of patients and staff. In the previous three years, 14,519 formally reported incidents involved interruptions to clinical services directly caused by poor building conditions, including power outages and faulty nurse‑call systems that delayed procedures such as planned caesarean sections.

A 2024 CQC report warned that many maternity units are not fit for purpose, lacking adequate space, facilities and, in some cases, essential life‑saving equipment, raising serious safety concerns for women and newborns.

St Helier Hospital in Sutton has been forced to relocate its maternity services because urgent repairs cannot be carried out while maintaining a safe environment for families. The trust’s chief executive said the scale of the required work makes it impossible to continue providing a good birth, gynaecology and fertility experience in the existing building.

Financial pressures compound the infrastructure crisis. In the latest budget, ministers trimmed £1 billion from the NHS capital budget over the next four years to fund defence spending, even as the estimated cost of clearing the NHS maintenance backlog has risen to £17.3 billion. The NHS Alliance chief executive highlighted that outdated, decaying buildings make it harder to deliver safe, high‑quality care, adding to existing staffing and service challenges.

The Department of Health and Social Care attributed the deteriorating state of many maternity units to a lack of maintenance under previous Conservative leadership, stating that the current government has invested £271 million since April 2025 on critical safety risks and announced more than £1.5 billion for broader NHS building improvements. It also noted a record capital budget for health rising to £15 billion by 2029‑30, with a ten‑year plan aimed at rebuilding facilities for mothers, babies and other patients.

Background: Maternity and neonatal units provide specialised care for pregnant women, newborns and infants, requiring reliable infrastructure such as stable power, functional medical equipment and appropriate space for delivery rooms, operating theatres and post‑natal care. Regulatory bodies like the Care Quality Commission inspect these facilities to ensure they meet safety and quality standards, reporting concerns that can trigger government action or funding allocations.

The Guardian reported on these developments, highlighting the gap between the known safety risks in maternity infrastructure and the government’s current inability to quantify the investment needed to address them.

articles.title: Patriots Face Potential Season‑Ending Ankle Injury to QB Drake Maye
articles.summary: Quarterback Drake Maye suffered a suspected fractured ankle in Week 10, likely sidelining him for the rest of the 2026 season, leaving New England to rely on backup Tommy DeVito.
articles.content:
New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye sustained a serious lower‑leg injury during the team’s Week 10 game against the Detroit Lions in Munich, Germany, according to a report from CBS Sports. The injury occurred on the final offensive snap of New England’s opening drive when Maye was sacked by pass rusher Aidan Hutchinson on a third‑and‑goal play. After the hit, Maye appeared in obvious discomfort, was examined on the sideline, and then walked gingerly to the locker room where he was later ruled out with an ankle injury.

Coach Mike Vrabel provided a brief update the following morning on Boston’s WEEI "The Greg Hill Show." He said, "The update that I have is just out of caution, Drake stayed back," and added that the quarterback would travel back to the United States once cleared. The statement indicated that Maye remained in Germany for additional testing, a detail that aligns with ESPN’s suggestion that the team fears a fractured ankle that could keep him out for the remainder of the season.

Maye’s statistical production through ten games this year reflects a mixed performance. He posted a 5‑5 record as a starter, completed 65.6 percent of his passes, averaged 233.0 passing yards per game, threw 18 touchdowns and 11 interceptions, the latter marking a career high. The Patriots, meanwhile, have slipped to a .500 record after losing three of their last four contests, dropping them from a No. 7 seed to the No. 8 seed in the AFC playoff picture. The loss to Detroit also widened the gap between New England and the AFC East leader, the Buffalo Bills, who sit at 8‑1.

Looking ahead, the Patriots face a challenging stretch that includes road games against the Bills, Vikings and Chiefs in December. Without Maye, the team would enter those matchups as significant underdogs, even though two of the three games are scheduled at Gillette Stadium.

In Maye’s absence, the Patriots will turn to backup quarterback Tommy DeVito, who entered the game against Detroit after Maye’s injury. DeVito completed 12 of 24 passes for 81 yards, recorded one touchdown and one interception, and added four rushes for 19 yards. He has been with New England for two seasons after being claimed off waivers in August 2025 following his release from the New York Giants. The team signed DeVito to a two‑year, $7.4 million extension last offseason, designating him as the primary backup entering the 2026 campaign.

DeVito, 28, entered the league in 2023 as an undrafted free agent from Illinois. He has started eight games in his career, posting a 3‑5 record, a 63.4 percent completion rate and an 84.6 passer rating. Those figures illustrate his limited but tangible experience as a starter, which the Patriots will need to leverage if Maye’s recovery extends beyond the season.

Background: A fractured ankle involves a break in one or more of the bones that make up the ankle joint. Recovery typically requires immobilization, possible surgical intervention, and a rehabilitation period that can span several months, depending on the severity and the specific bones involved. In the NFL, the loss of a starting quarterback often forces a team to rely on its backup, who must quickly adapt to the starter’s game plan and maintain offensive continuity.

Background: The role of a backup quarterback extends beyond simply filling in for the starter. Backups must stay prepared through the week, study the playbook, and be ready to execute the team’s offensive scheme with limited live-game repetitions. Their performance can influence a team’s ability to remain competitive, especially during stretches with multiple high‑stakes games.

The Patriots have a bye week in Week 11, providing a brief window for medical staff to assess Maye’s condition and for the coaching staff to prepare DeVito for the upcoming schedule. As of the latest information, no definitive timeline has been given for Maye’s return, and the team’s immediate focus remains on stabilizing its offense and preserving its playoff aspirations despite the setback.

articles.title: Retailers Embrace Entertainment to Capture Consumer Attention
articles.summary: Retailers are adding entertainment, content and experiential elements to their brands to engage shoppers, with Gap leading the trend through a new chief entertainment officer role, while experts note the growing value of intellectual property.
articles.content:
Gap Inc. created a chief entertainment officer position earlier this year and hired former Paramount executive Pam Kaufman to lead its entertainment, content and licensing efforts. Since her arrival, the company has launched high‑profile campaigns that feature musical acts such as Just Your Type and have built on prior advertising that highlighted the girl group Katseye. Kaufman explained that beloved brands possess value beyond the items they sell, noting that authenticity is essential for any brand extension to resonate with fans.

The strategy Gap calls "fashiontainment" blends retail with entertainment, aiming to align the brand more closely with consumer culture. CEO Richard Dickson has described the approach as placing the company’s brands at the center of cultural conversation, a theme he reiterated at a recent consumer conference. The move mirrors earlier examples of retail‑media convergence, such as Mattel’s successful "Barbie" film, which leveraged a long‑standing intellectual property to generate significant box‑office revenue while Dickson was serving as the toy maker’s president and chief operating officer.

Industry observers say the shift reflects a broader change in shopper behavior that accelerated after the pandemic. Bryan Eshelman of AlixPartners observes that consumers now view shopping as an entertainment experience rather than a purely transactional task. Retailers are responding by offering community‑focused initiatives, lifestyle content and a sense of belonging that extend beyond the products themselves.

Branded entertainment has deep roots in advertising history. In the 1930s, Procter & Gamble helped popularize the term "soap opera" as a way to embed product messages within serialized storytelling. Over the decades, companies have continued to produce media campaigns designed to attract customers, but the rise of social platforms and short‑form video has intensified demand for fresh, original content.

Experts highlight that intellectual property (IP) has become a critical asset in this environment. Alex Michael, senior managing director at LionTree, told CNBC, "IP, in that sense, is the most valuable thing out there, and only becoming more valuable because it's attached to audience." He added that IP now spans video, audio, short‑form, long‑form and live events, requiring brands to engage consumers earlier in the purchase journey to earn trust.

Cross‑industry experience appears to be a valuable commodity. Kaufman's background in film and television, as well as the previous entertainment roles held by Dickson and Skydance co‑CEO Ynon Kreiz at Mattel, illustrate how expertise in both retail and media can help navigate the blurred lines between the sectors. Michael notes that professionals who can operate across these domains are increasingly sought after as the definitions of retail, media, entertainment and live events converge.

The evolving landscape also opens opportunities for newer entrants. Sean Akaks, chief executive of SonderCo, points out that consolidation among legacy studios is creating more space for independent creators and brands to produce content outside traditional studio systems. He envisions a future where creators and brands co‑create IP and share ownership of the resulting assets.

Retailers are leveraging these collaborations to drive foot traffic and deepen in‑store experiences. For example, Dick’s Sporting Goods has introduced interactive activities and simulators within its locations, turning shopping trips into immersive events. Data from AlixPartners indicates that firms investing in experiential retail, such as Coach and Ralph Lauren, have seen average basket sizes rise by close to 10% year over year.

Jeff Goldstein of AlixPartners explains that combining distributed electronic content with on‑site experiences creates a feedback loop similar to the "flywheel" effect pursued by entertainment companies. By using digital media to attract shoppers and then delivering a compelling physical environment, retailers aim to sustain engagement and repeat visits.

Nevertheless, entertainment initiatives are only one component of a successful retail strategy. Eshelman emphasizes that core fundamentals—having desirable products, transparent pricing and reliable inventory—remain essential. Glitzy experiences cannot compensate for weak merchandise or poor value propositions.

Background: Branded entertainment refers to the creation of media content that promotes a brand’s identity, values or products, often through storytelling, music, film or digital series. This approach seeks to embed the brand within cultural moments, making it part of consumers’ everyday media consumption.

Background: Experiential retail focuses on designing store environments that offer interactive, sensory or participatory elements, encouraging shoppers to spend more time in the space and fostering emotional connections that go beyond the transaction.

As retailers continue to experiment with entertainment and immersive experiences, the industry’s ability to capture attention will depend on balancing innovative content with the underlying quality of the products they sell.

articles.title: Georgia dominates, Wake Forest soars while Kentucky’s playoff hopes fade
articles.summary: Week 11 saw No. 1 Georgia and No. 13 Wake Forest reinforce their elite status, while Kentucky’s loss to Florida likely ends its CFP bid, CBS Sports reports.
articles.content:
Georgia continued its march toward a national championship claim by delivering a decisive victory over Missouri, building a 31-0 lead early and finishing with a 48-21 win. The Bulldogs’ ground attack, highlighted by three touchdowns from running back Nate Frazier, complemented a defense that has allowed just fifteen points across the last three games. Over roughly ten quarters of play, Georgia has outscored opponents by a wide margin, underscoring the consistency that has kept it atop the rankings.

Wake Forest added another impressive performance to its résumé, crushing SMU 49-7. The Demon Deacons surged to a 42-0 advantage before halftime, showcasing dominance in both the passing and rushing phases. Quarterback Gio Lopez has been a model of efficiency, posting nineteen touchdown passes against a single interception in recent outings. The comprehensive victory against a traditionally strong SMU defense further cemented Wake Forest’s place among the week’s top performers.

In contrast, Kentucky’s season took a sharp turn after a narrow 21-14 defeat to Florida. The Wildcats surrendered a fourteen‑play touchdown drive in the final quarter and were unable to convert four consecutive fourth‑down attempts. The loss effectively extinguished the team’s chances of reaching the College Football Playoff, opening the field for other contenders. Coach Will Stein, who had risen to national coach‑of‑the‑year consideration, now faces a dramatically altered postseason outlook.

The Big 12 delivered notable storylines, with No. 2 Utah overcoming logistical challenges to secure a 40-39 win over Arizona. After a flight cancellation forced the team to travel early, quarterback Devon Dampier threw for 200 yards and added a rushing contribution that helped the Utes rally in the fourth quarter. The narrow victory kept Utah unbeaten and positioned it as a potential challenger for the top overall spot.

Texas Tech rebounded from a close call against West Virginia by defeating No. 25 Oklahoma State 52-27. Transfer quarterback Thomas Castellanos accounted for 263 yards and four touchdowns, while the defense produced a second‑half shutout against a high‑scoring conference opponent. The win revitalized the Red Raiders’ postseason prospects and signaled a return to competitiveness within the Big 12.

New Mexico’s playoff aspirations were dashed after a 21-17 loss to UNLV. Former five‑star quarterback Jackson Arnold capped the game with a 44‑yard run, securing a victory for Dan Mullen’s staff. The Lobos had already fallen behind in the CFP race, and the defeat likely cements their position outside the playoff conversation.

USC’s performance remained uneven, highlighted by a victory over Ohio State but offset by a 27-13 loss to Indiana. Indiana’s quarterback Grant Wilson, in his first start, threw for 305 yards and two touchdowns, exposing vulnerabilities in the Trojans’ defense. The Trojans have struggled to dominate ranked opponents, with narrow margins of victory in their other Big Ten contests.

Iowa State’s running back Aidan Flora continued his breakout stretch, rushing for 216 yards and three touchdowns, marking his third consecutive game with at least 180 yards. His production has propelled the Cyclones toward bowl eligibility, emphasizing the impact a single playmaker can have on a program’s fortunes.

Wisconsin’s season took a downturn after a 24-21 loss to Maryland, a game in which the Badgers surrendered a late lead and fell short despite a strong defensive effort earlier. The defeat marked the team’s second loss in three games and raised questions about the program’s trajectory given recent investments.

Georgia Tech found a rare bright spot by defeating Clemson 20-6, the first victory over the Tigers since 2008. Coach Brent Key’s recent staff changes appeared to pay off, as the defense limited Clemson to six points and a modest rushing total.

Background: In college football, the College Football Playoff (CFP) selects the top four teams to compete for the national championship, with rankings influencing bowl game invitations and postseason matchups. Teams strive to secure wins against ranked opponents to improve their standing and increase the likelihood of a playoff berth.

Background: A fourth‑quarter comeback refers to a team overcoming a deficit in the final period of play, often requiring a combination of offensive efficiency and defensive stops to reverse the game's momentum.

CBS Sports reported these developments, highlighting the shifting landscape as the season approaches its climax.

articles.title: Hundreds of English Children Prescribed Weight‑Loss GLP‑1 Injections, Data Reveal
articles.summary: A Guardian investigation found over 400 prescriptions for GLP‑1 weight‑loss drugs were issued to English children in 2025‑26, including a small number under twelve, prompting calls for specialist oversight.
articles.content:
An investigation by The Guardian has uncovered that hundreds of children in England are being prescribed GLP‑1 medications, drugs originally created to manage blood‑sugar levels in type‑2 diabetes but now widely used as weight‑loss treatments.

The data, obtained through freedom‑of‑information requests to the NHS Business Services Authority, show that in the financial year 2025‑26 a total of 419 prescriptions were issued to patients under 18, with ten of those for children younger than 12. In the four‑month period from April to July of the same year, 341 prescriptions were recorded for children, fifteen of them for those under 12.

These figures only reflect prescriptions dispensed in community settings across the United Kingdom and exclude private prescriptions, hospital‑based supplies and prescriptions issued in prisons, meaning the true number of young patients receiving the drugs is likely higher.

A private clinic that treats children has previously disclosed that more than 200 of its patients are receiving the injections, although it is not clear whether all of those prescriptions are intended solely for weight loss.

Professor Martin Whyte, a metabolic‑medicine specialist at the University of Surrey, noted that while the absolute number of prescriptions is modest compared with the scale of childhood obesity, any child started on a GLP‑1 drug must be managed within specialist services that monitor growth, puberty, nutrition, mental health and potential side effects. He warned that weight often returns after treatment stops and that long‑term safety data in growing bodies remain limited.

Background: GLP‑1 (glucagon‑like peptide‑1) agonists work by mimicking a gut hormone that increases insulin secretion, slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite, which together can lead to weight loss. They are administered by injection and have become prominent in adult obesity treatment in recent years.

Childhood obesity rates continue to rise. The National Child Measurement Programme reports that roughly one in ten reception‑year pupils (aged four to five) are classified as obese, a proportion that climbs to almost one in four children in year 6 (aged ten to eleven). The World Health Organization estimates that hundreds of millions of children and adolescents worldwide are overweight or obese.

In response to the growing problem, the NHS began piloting Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics in 2021, targeting children aged two to 16 with severe obesity. By May, almost 6,500 children had been referred to these clinics, including more than 400 younger than four, and a number of them have received GLP‑1 therapy through hospital pharmacies where funding is available.

Dr Dunia Ismail, a consultant paediatrician who runs a CEW clinic, said that clinicians are now considering extending treatment to children as young as eight once the medication gains formal licence approval.

Global guidance from the WHO released last month advises that obesity medicines should not be given to children under ten years of age. Nevertheless, a trial conducted by Novo Nordisk involving 165 participants aged six to just under twelve suggested that GLP‑1 drugs can be effective for younger children with obesity.

Professor Julian Hamilton‑Shield, who works at the Bristol CEW clinic, explained that GLP‑1 therapy is typically offered only after standard dietary advice, nutritional counselling and psychological support have failed, and most of the children treated have serious co‑morbidities such as type 2 diabetes, sleep apnoea or liver disease. He described the condition as comparable to morbid obesity in adults.

"We’re a health service that delivers health to the people who require it. We’re not one that makes moral judgments about people," Hamilton‑Shield said, emphasizing that treatment decisions are based on clinical need rather than weight alone.

He added that for many young patients the medication can produce dramatic weight loss of 25 kg or more, restoring a sense of agency and potentially improving self‑esteem and social participation.

Dr Ismail reiterated that obesity is a medical condition, not a lifestyle choice, and that without effective intervention children face a high risk of early heart disease, diabetes and premature death.

The emerging use of GLP‑1 drugs in paediatric care has reignited discussion about the causes of childhood obesity, but experts agree that any expansion of prescribing must be accompanied by specialist supervision, comprehensive monitoring and a clear plan for long‑term health outcomes.

articles.title: Nationwide FAA Ground Stop Sends US Airports into Turmoil
articles.summary: A sudden FAA-ordered ground stop halted flights across the United States, leaving thousands of travelers stranded and prompting widespread confusion at major hubs.
articles.content:
The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop on a Friday afternoon, forcing all departures to cease and plunging airports from coast to coast into disorder. Passengers who were already in terminals or on board aircraft found themselves in an unexpected limbo as the directive took effect, with airlines scrambling to communicate the evolving situation.

At New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport, the disruption was palpable. Steve Honberger, who was returning to Portland with his family, described how his flight was still at the gate when the shutdown was announced. He recalled the crew’s uncertainty, saying, "They didn’t seem to know what’s happening, and they wanted to hold off as long as possible," and noted that the aircraft remained parked for more than an hour before passengers were allowed to deplane and seek alternative arrangements.

Other travelers shared similar stories of uncertainty. Rashid Kahn, bound for Miami, recalled hearing about the ground stop on the news and receiving a vague estimate from his airline that the flight might depart late in the evening. Tom Rolenaitis, who was transporting a show dog back to Finland, expressed frustration at the interruption to a three‑day itinerary. An unnamed flight attendant on an American Airlines service to Barcelona reported a brief delay notice, while a fellow crew member remained hopeful that the situation would resolve without further incident.

As the afternoon progressed, some international flights began to board, prompting applause from passengers at the gates. An airline representative observed that only inbound international services were being cleared to land, indicating a partial restoration of operations.

The FAA’s notice cited communication problems at regional air‑traffic control centers as the trigger for the stop. Approximately four hours later, the agency issued an advisory indicating that the restriction was being lifted, allowing airlines to resume departures where possible.

The aftermath of the lift generated additional confusion. Larson Welsh, traveling from Paris to Las Vegas, described how his flight was first cancelled, then re‑scheduled for an early‑morning departure via an automated kiosk, only to encounter staff who appeared unaware of the new itinerary.

Flight tracking data showed more than ten thousand delays and nearly fifteen hundred cancellations linked to the event, while over a thousand aircraft were en route to the United States when the stop was announced. These figures underscore the scale of the disruption for both domestic and inbound traffic.

National ground stops are exceedingly rare. Prior to this incident, only two such orders had been issued: one following the September 2001 terrorist attacks and another in early 2023 after a communications failure. The rarity of the measure highlights the seriousness with which the FAA regarded the underlying technical issue.

The ripple effects extended beyond commercial passengers. Sports leagues, including the NBA, NHL, and collegiate programs, faced logistical challenges as teams and officials struggled to reach venues for a busy weekend of games. The uncertainty around referee travel added another layer of complication for organizers.

Background: A ground stop is an air‑traffic control directive that temporarily halts departures from a specified area or, in the case of a national order, from all airports within a country. The purpose is to manage air‑space capacity and ensure safety when the system cannot safely handle the usual volume of traffic, often due to technical failures or extreme weather.

Background: When flights are cancelled or delayed, airlines typically use automated kiosks, online platforms, and customer‑service desks to rebook passengers on later services. The process can involve reassigning seats, issuing new boarding passes, and sometimes arranging accommodation for stranded travelers.

Back at JFK, frustration was evident. A passenger identified only as Andy lamented that his flight to California had been cancelled without any information or rebooking options, adding, "It’s frustrating. And I’m pissed." His comments reflected the broader sentiment of travelers who missed personal events and faced uncertain onward travel.

Despite the challenges, some passengers tried to maintain a positive outlook. Honberger noted that seeing other aircraft still on the tarmac offered a measure of reassurance, and he was able to secure a hotel room for the night, describing the experience as a mix of luck and resilience.

articles.sourceTitle: ‘It’s frustrating’: chaos at US airports as stoppage grinds travel plans to a halt

articles.title: English teen boxer barred from World Championships after sex‑test oversight
articles.summary: Eighteen‑year‑old George Francis was excluded from the Under‑19 World Championships in Montenegro when England Boxing failed to arrange a required sex verification test, leaving him unable to compete.
articles.content:
George Francis, an 18‑year‑old boxer from Loughton, Essex, was set to represent England in the 60kg division at the Under‑19 World Championships in Budva, Montenegro. Hours before the competition draw, he was told he could not take part because officials could not confirm his sex status.

Francis explained the moment he was informed, saying, "They got me in a room and told me that I couldn't box because they didn't know if I was a boy or a girl, basically,". The explanation given was that a blood sample required for verification could not be provided in time, a step that other athletes had completed.

According to Francis, the oversight stemmed from an administrative error by England Boxing, which left his name absent from the system used to schedule the required testing. He added that there were no qualified doctors in Budva to conduct the test, and the missed deadline meant he was deemed ineligible.

The young athlete described the news as the worst he had ever received, saying he felt "broken" and could not process the information. He recounted being unable to speak or feel anything after hearing the decision, emphasizing the emotional toll of the sudden exclusion.

Francis is a multiple schoolboy and junior national champion who had been training continuously for the chance to compete at his first senior world event. The opportunity was also seen as a stepping stone toward Olympic qualification, a goal now out of reach after the incident.

In the wake of the setback, Francis said he is considering turning professional, expressing that he sees little future for himself as an amateur. He noted that he turned 18 only four days before his scheduled departure, suggesting the timing may have contributed to the missed verification.

His father, who has been contacted by England Boxing, reported that he has not received any direct communication from the governing body regarding the matter. He expressed frustration at being left without a phone call or message, questioning how the situation was allowed to occur.

England Boxing issued a statement acknowledging the administrative oversight and describing the steps taken once the issue was identified. The body said it worked with competition organisers to explore options under World Boxing regulations, maintained communication with Francis and his family, but could not reach a resolution. It affirmed that Francis remained a valued member of the England squad, even serving as a flag bearer, and reiterated its commitment to athlete health and process improvement.

Sex verification testing in boxing is intended to confirm that competitors meet the gender eligibility criteria set by the sport's governing bodies. The process typically involves the collection of a biological sample, such as blood, which is then analysed to determine genetic sex. National federations are responsible for ensuring that athletes complete the required testing before international events.

World Boxing introduced mandatory genetic sex testing for female competitors aged 18 and above last year, citing safety and a level playing field as reasons for the policy. In January, the organisation extended the requirement to include male boxers, making the verification process universal across genders.

The policy change followed controversy at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where two female gold‑medalists had previously been disqualified from the prior World Championships after failing sex eligibility tests administered by the former International Boxing Association. The incident highlighted inconsistencies in testing procedures and prompted calls for clearer, more consistent regulations.

A similar issue arose in 2025 when a group of female fighters from several nations were barred from the World Championships in Liverpool because the deadlines for their sex tests were missed. That episode underscored the importance of timely administration of verification protocols.

BBC Sport reported on Francis's case, noting that the boxer now faces an uncertain future in the amateur ranks. He has called for stronger safeguards to prevent similar administrative failures, urging that a dedicated individual oversee the testing process to protect athletes from repeat mistakes.

The incident has sparked discussion within the boxing community about the balance between safeguarding competition integrity and ensuring athletes are not unfairly excluded due to bureaucratic errors. England Boxing has pledged to learn from the experience and strengthen its procedures, aiming to avoid another scenario where a promising young boxer is left without the chance to compete on the world stage.

articles.title: UK services disrupted by global Microsoft outage affecting NHS, schools and police
articles.summary: A worldwide Microsoft service failure has interrupted email, messaging and cloud tools, impacting health services, education, law enforcement and other public and private sectors across the United Kingdom, according to BBC News.
articles.content:
A massive interruption to Microsoft’s online suite has rippled through a range of essential services in the United Kingdom. The outage, which began early on the day of reporting, has taken down Outlook, Teams and the newer Copilot feature, leaving millions of users without access to core communication and scheduling tools. Microsoft has indicated that the problem stemmed from an unusually high load on its servers, causing many to become unavailable and over‑burdening the remaining infrastructure. While the company says restoration is progressing, some users continue to experience intermittent disruption.

Health providers have felt the impact most acutely. NHS England urged patients to keep attending appointments unless they receive direct instruction otherwise, and stressed that emergency lines – 999 for life‑threatening cases and 111 for non‑urgent medical advice – remain operational. Several GP surgeries, including those in Hampshire and Shropshire, asked patients to avoid using online contact forms and to call or visit in person for urgent matters. The NHS Alliance chief executive confirmed that email services used by the health system were among those affected, prompting trusts to activate contingency measures aimed at preserving critical care pathways.

The disruption has also complicated pharmacy operations. A spokesperson for the National Pharmacy Association noted that the inability to exchange messages with GP practices could lengthen waiting times for prescriptions and cause delays in patient communication. In parallel, the GMB union’s national secretary, Rachel Harrison, warned that ambulance and NHS trust staff were unable to transmit patient details through their usual channels, creating a substantial backlog and raising the risk of chaos, although emergency call‑outs appeared to be unaffected.

Law‑enforcement agencies across England, Wales and Scotland reported similar challenges. The Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland all indicated that online reporting forms were compromised, prompting officers to advise the public to call for any time‑critical, non‑emergency concerns. This advice aimed to ensure that crime reporting could continue despite the loss of digital submission routes.

Local government bodies also faced interruptions. The Local Government Association cautioned that some council services might be disrupted but affirmed that plans were in place to maintain essential support for residents. Downing Street said officials were working closely with Microsoft to obtain a comprehensive picture of the outage’s reach within government operations.

Educational institutions have been forced to adapt quickly. Teachers, administrative staff and parents in schools reported being unable to access calendars, email accounts and internal cloud storage, hampering routine coordination. One head teacher near Newcastle described how safeguarding systems were offline, requiring staff to record concerns manually. Another head teacher in Cheshire explained that the delay forced the postponement of termly school reports. Universities, including the University of Portsmouth and the University of Aberdeen, reported interruptions to platforms used for assignment submissions, leading some to extend deadlines or waive penalties for late work.

Higher education is not the only sector turning to workarounds. Businesses ranging from small enterprises to larger firms have reverted to paper records or shifted communication to alternative platforms such as WhatsApp. A PR agency owner in Kent described the outage as causing "huge disruption" because she could not send pitches or invoices. A baker and wine bar owner expressed concern that the loss of online tools threatened pre‑Christmas sales, while a resident in Stirlingshire was unable to retrieve tickets for a rugby match.

Parliamentary functions have also been hindered. Members of Parliament reported being locked out of their parliamentary accounts, though a spokesperson said temporary arrangements were in place to allow continued work. In Scotland, the government activated its "resilience operations" to assess the impact, and Members of the Scottish Parliament confirmed that Holyrood’s email systems were down, limiting communication with constituents and urgent casework.

The scale of the outage is underscored by the fact that roughly 430 million people worldwide rely on Microsoft’s online tools. The interconnected nature of the affected services means that a failure in one component can cascade across multiple organisations, amplifying the overall disruption.

Background: Outlook is a widely used email client that integrates calendar and contact management, while Teams provides chat, video conferencing and file‑sharing capabilities for collaborative work. Both platforms are often embedded in organisational workflows, making them critical for daily operations in sectors ranging from health care to education.

Background: A cyber‑attack involves malicious actors deliberately targeting computer systems to steal data, disrupt services or cause damage. In this incident, Microsoft and independent security experts have ruled out such an attack, attributing the outage to technical overload rather than hostile activity.

Cyber‑security adviser Jake Moore explained the technical dynamics, stating, "Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes." He highlighted that the sudden concentration of traffic on fewer servers caused a slowdown and eventual failure of services. Moore told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the event underscores the importance of having independent contingency communication networks that do not rely on a single provider.

Industry observers note that many organisations have built redundancy into their digital ecosystems, but the reliance on a handful of major platforms can still produce significant knock‑on effects when those platforms falter. Nicky Choo of Mimecast confirmed that while their firm uses Microsoft tools, they maintain alternative channels to mitigate disruption.

The immediate priority for affected entities remains maintaining essential services. Health providers continue to advise patients to use emergency numbers, while police forces encourage phone contact for urgent matters. Schools and universities are adjusting reporting and assessment timelines where possible. Government departments are collaborating with Microsoft to gauge the full extent of the impact and to restore normal operations.

As restoration efforts continue, users are advised to anticipate intermittent performance and to consider temporary communication methods where feasible. The incident serves as a reminder of the vulnerabilities inherent in heavily integrated digital infrastructures and the need for robust backup strategies across public and private sectors.
